title: AWS Databases Revision Notes: RDS and DynamoDB
summary: Quick revision of RDS engines, Multi-AZ vs read replicas and backups, then DynamoDB keys, GSIs and capacity modes, ending with when to choose which.

chapters.title: What This Handbook Covers
points: RDS engines and Aurora
Multi-AZ vs read replicas
Automated backups and snapshots
DynamoDB keys and GSIs
Capacity modes and RDS vs DynamoDB

chapters.title: RDS Engines, Multi-AZ and Read Replicas
points: RDS is a managed relational database with no OS or SSH access. Engines: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Db2, and Aurora (MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible, 6 copies across 3 AZs, storage grows to 256 TiB on current versions).
Multi-AZ instance deployment: a synchronous standby in another AZ. On failure RDS flips the same DNS endpoint to the standby automatically (roughly 1-2 minutes). The standby serves no reads.

Read replica: asynchronous copy with its own endpoint, used to scale reads. Up to 15 for MySQL/PostgreSQL/MariaDB (5 for Oracle and SQL Server) and 15 for Aurora. It can be cross-Region, and it can be promoted to a standalone DB. Replication lag is possible.

Comparison: Multi-AZ is synchronous, same Region, for HA/DR and has no reads. A read replica is asynchronous, can be cross-Region, for read scaling and has no automatic failover. A Multi-AZ DB cluster (two readable standbys) is the exception.

Common mistakes: counting a read replica as your failover, sending writes to a replica, and expecting strictly fresh reads from async replicas. Interview Point: (1) Is Multi-AZ a scaling feature? (2) How do you add cross-Region DR for reads? (3) Why does a replica read return stale data? (4) What happens to the endpoint on failover?

chapters.title: RDS Backups and Recovery
points: Automated backups: a daily snapshot plus transaction logs, on by default with 7 days of retention (configurable 1-35). Point-in-time restore works to any second within the window. Setting retention to 0 turns them off.
Manual snapshots persist until you delete them and survive instance deletion. Automated backups are removed with the instance unless you choose to retain them.
A restore never overwrites the instance. It always creates a new instance with a new endpoint, so you must repoint the application.
Snapshots can be copied across Regions and shared across accounts. Encryption cannot be removed: to encrypt an unencrypted DB, copy its snapshot with a KMS key and restore from the copy.

Common mistakes: expecting an in-place restore, relying on automated backups after deleting the DB, and disabling backups on a source DB that has read replicas. Interview Point: (1) Automated backup vs manual snapshot? (2) How do you recover from a bad DELETE 10 minutes ago? (3) How do you encrypt an existing unencrypted RDS DB?

chapters.title: DynamoDB Tables, Keys and GSIs
points: DynamoDB is serverless key-value/document NoSQL with single-digit-millisecond latency and a 400 KB item limit. The primary key is either a partition key alone or partition key + sort key (composite).
The partition key is hashed to pick the physical partition. Use a high-cardinality, evenly accessed key. A low-cardinality or skewed key (e.g. status, date) creates a hot partition and throttling.
The sort key orders items within a partition. Query reads one partition key and can add begins_with, between or ordering. Scan reads the whole table and is slow and costly, so avoid it in production.

GSI: a different partition and sort key, with its own capacity, eventually consistent reads only, up to 20 per table, addable anytime. LSI: same partition key with a different sort key, creatable only at table creation, up to 5, with a 10 GB-per-partition limit.
Interview Point: (1) How do you query by an attribute that is not the key? (2) Query vs Scan? (3) GSI vs LSI? (4) How do you avoid a hot partition?

chapters.title: Capacity Modes and Choosing RDS vs DynamoDB
points: On-demand mode: pay per request, no capacity planning, and it absorbs spikes. It suits new or unpredictable traffic.

Provisioned mode: you set RCU and WCU, with auto scaling available, and it is cheaper for steady, predictable traffic. 1 RCU = one strongly consistent 4 KB read per second (two eventually consistent). 1 WCU = one 1 KB write per second.

You can switch from provisioned to on-demand up to four times in a rolling 24-hour window, and from on-demand to provisioned at any time. Exceeding provisioned throughput raises ProvisionedThroughputExceededException, so use retries with backoff.

Choose RDS for joins, large or complex relational transactions, ad-hoc SQL and existing engine compatibility. Choose DynamoDB for known access patterns, key lookups, massive scale and predictable latency, and design the table around those queries.

Common mistake: modelling DynamoDB like a relational schema and then needing Scans. Interview Point: (1) On-demand vs provisioned? (2) How many RCUs for 100 strongly consistent 8 KB reads per second? (3) When would you not use DynamoDB?

chapters.title: AWS Databases Cheat Sheet
points: HA: Multi-AZ, synchronous, auto failover, no reads. Read scaling: read replicas, asynchronous, promotable, cross-Region.
Backups: automated 1-35 days (default 7) with PITR; manual snapshots persist; every restore creates a new instance.
DynamoDB keys: the partition key is hashed and must be even; the sort key enables Query ranges; avoid Scan. GSI is anytime and eventually consistent; LSI only at creation.
Capacity: on-demand for unpredictable traffic; provisioned for steady traffic. 1 RCU = 4 KB strongly consistent read/s; 1 WCU = 1 KB write/s.
Interview Point: (1) Multi-AZ vs read replica? (2) GSI vs LSI? (3) RDS or DynamoDB for this workload, and why?
